title: Indicator tricks
objectives: Solve counting expectations with indicator variables.

screens.title: Count the runs
screens.prose: Ten flips of a coin. A **run** is a block of equal faces in a row: HH, T, H, TTT, HH, T.
screens.question: Tap every flip that starts a new run.

hints.text: Flip 3 is a T after an H, so it starts a run.
Flip 1, then the changes at 3, 4, 5, 8 and 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A run starts at the first flip, and wherever a flip differs from the one before.

byKey.no-first: You found every change. Flip 1 starts a run too, though nothing comes before it.

explain.text: The runs number $1 + 5 = 6$: one for flip 1 and one for each change. So counting runs is counting changes. Each change is a yes-or-no event at one place.

screens.title: Expected runs
screens.prose: Mark flip $k$ with $I_k = 1$ if it differs from flip $k - 1$, else 0. A 0-or-1 marker like this is an **indicator**. Then the runs number $1 + I_2 + \dots + I_{10}$.
screens.question: How many runs do you expect in 10 fair flips? Give one decimal place.

hints.text: Nine: one for each of flips 2 to 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each of flips 2 to 10 differs from the one before with chance $\tfrac12$.

byKey.half: You gave all 10 flips a chance of $\tfrac12$ to start a run. Flip 1 always starts one.
byKey.ten: You counted a change at flip 1. Only flips 2 to 10 have a flip before them.

explain.text: $E[I_k] = P(\text{flip } k \text{ differs}) = \tfrac12$, so $E[\text{runs}] = 1 + 9 \times \tfrac12 = 5.5$. We never needed the chance of exactly 6 runs. Expectation passes through the sum term by term.

screens.title: Empty boxes
screens.prose: Now a count with ten indicators. Throw 10 balls at random into 10 boxes, each ball landing in any box with chance $\tfrac1{10}$. The grid shows one throw.

state.caption: One throw of 10 balls: the balls that landed in each box.

screens.question: How many boxes do you expect to stay empty? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Box 1 stays empty when all 10 balls miss it, chance $0.9^{10}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance one box stays empty, then add over the boxes.

byKey.one-box: That is the chance one box stays empty. There are ten boxes.
byKey.none: Ten balls for ten boxes rarely fill every box: some boxes catch two or more.

explain.text: Box $j$ is empty with chance $0.9^{10} \approx 0.3487$, so about 3.49 of the 10 boxes stay empty. The throw shown has 4 empty boxes, close to that.

screens.title: Shared birthdays
screens.prose: Thirty people, with birthdays spread evenly over 365 days. Give each **pair** of people an indicator: 1 if they share a birthday.

state.caption: Six of the 30 people. Each line is one pair: 15 lines for six people.

screens.question: How many pairs do you expect to share a birthday? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: How many pairs do 30 people make?
Six people make 15 pairs, as the lines show.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pairs, then multiply by one pair's chance.

byKey.people: You gave each person an indicator. A shared birthday belongs to a pair.
byKey.ordered: You counted each pair twice, as Ann with Bo and Bo with Ann.
byKey.at-least: That is the chance at least one pair matches. The question asks for the expected number of pairs.

explain.text: Each of the 435 pairs matches with chance $\tfrac1{365}$, so $E = 435/365 \approx 1.19$. The pair indicators are dependent: if Ann matches Bo and Bo matches Cai, Ann matches Cai. Linearity adds them anyway.

screens.title: But they are dependent
screens.prose: A candidate objects: the empty-box indicators depend on each other. If nine boxes are empty, the tenth cannot be. So $10 \times 0.9^{10}$ must be wrong.

state.caption: One throw of 10 balls: the balls that landed in each box.

screens.question: Is $10 \times 0.9^{10}$ the expected number of empty boxes?

options.text: No: dependence makes it too large
options.why: Dependence changes the spread of the count, not its mean. $E[I_1 + I_2] = E[I_1] + E[I_2]$ always.

options.text: No: you need $P(k \text{ empty})$ for every $k$ first
options.why: That is the full distribution: hours of work for the same answer. Only the mean is asked.
It is exact for any number of boxes. Linearity is an identity, not an approximation.

hints.text: Does $E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]$ need anything about $X$ and $Y$?
Linearity holds for any random variables.
So the dependent indicators still add: $10 \times 0.9^{10}$.

feedback.correct: Yes. $E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]$ for any $X$ and $Y$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether linearity of expectation ever needs independence.

byKey.b: You let the dependence move the mean. It moves the variance; the mean is still $10 \times 0.9^{10}$.
byKey.c: You went for the full distribution. When only the expectation is asked, sum the indicators and stop.

explain.text: Expectation is a weighted sum, and sums can be reordered whatever the dependence. So $E[\sum I_j] = \sum E[I_j]$ holds exactly. Refusing to add, or reaching for the distribution, wastes the interview.

screens.title: Where pairs come back
screens.prose: Linearity gives every expected count. A spread is another matter: $$\text{Var}(N) = \sum_k \text{Var}(I_k) + 2\sum_{j<k} \text{Cov}(I_j, I_k).$$

state.caption: One throw of 10 balls: the balls that landed in each box.

screens.question: For the empty boxes, which of these needs the chance that two given boxes are both empty?

options.why: The mean needs one box at a time: $0.9^{10}$ each.
That is $10 - E[N]$, still one box at a time.

feedback.correct: Only the variance needs pairs: $P(\text{boxes } j \text{ and } k \text{ empty}) = 0.8^{10}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which expression has a product of two indicators in it?

explain.text: Every linear expression in $N$ needs only single boxes. The variance has cross terms $E[I_jI_k] = 0.8^{10}$, the chance both boxes are empty. This is the edge case: indicators give means at once, but spreads need pairs.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: Every count here was a sum of indicators. If $N$ counts which of the events $A_1, \dots, A_n$ happen, $$E[N] = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + \dots + P(A_n),$$ however the events depend on each other.
screens.question: Which step of the rule needs the events to be independent?

options.why: Linearity holds for any random variables, dependent or not.
Each chance is found alone, one event at a time.

feedback.correct: None. That is why the trick is so quick.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Linearity never asks about dependence.

explain.text: $E[I_k] = P(A_k)$ because an indicator is 1 with chance $P(A_k)$ and 0 otherwise. Linearity adds these whatever the dependence. So the hard part is only choosing what each indicator marks.

screens.title: Aces before the first king
screens.prose: Shuffle a deck of 52 cards. We want the expected number of aces that come before the first king.
screens.question: Put the argument in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Give ace $j$ an indicator: $I_j = 1$ when it comes before all four kings.
Look only at ace $j$ and the four kings: each of these five is equally likely to come first.
The indicators are dependent, so multiply their chances: $(\tfrac15)^4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Define the indicators before finding their chances.

byKey.d1: Multiplying chances gives the chance all four aces beat the kings. The expected count adds the chances.
byKey.left-out: All four true lines are needed.
byKey.s2: Choose what the indicator marks before finding its chance.

explain.text: The other 47 cards do not matter for whether ace $j$ beats the kings. Among ace $j$ and the kings, each is first with chance $\tfrac15$. Adding four indicators gives $0.8$.

screens.title: New highs in a month
screens.prose: A toy model: a strategy's 21 daily closes in a month arrive in random order, all different. Day $k$ is a new high for the month if it beats days 1 to $k - 1$.

state.caption: In the toy model, day $k$ is a new high for the month with chance $1/k$.

screens.question: How many new highs do you expect in the month, counting day 1? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: By symmetry, any of the first $k$ closes is equally likely to be the largest.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Day $k$ is the largest of the first $k$ closes with chance $1/k$.

byKey.half: You gave each day an even chance. A late day must beat many earlier ones.
byKey.one: That counts only the month's final high. Every earlier record counts too.
byKey.log: That is $\ln 21$, a close estimate of the sum, not the sum itself.

explain.text: Day $k$ is a new high with chance $1/k$, so $E = H_{21} \approx 3.65$. Real prices trend and cluster, so a desk would test this against data. The indicator view still sets the baseline in one line.

ideas: Write the count as a sum of indicators, one for each place an event might happen.
The expected count is the sum of the events' chances, whatever the dependence between them.
A variance needs pairs of indicators; a mean never does.
summary.trap: Refusing to add dependent indicators, or working out the full distribution when only the mean is asked.

quiz.prose: Flip a fair coin 10 times. Count every place where two heads stand side by side, overlaps included: HHH holds two.
quiz.question: What is the expected count? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. There are 9 places for a pair, each HH with chance $\tfrac14$.

byKey.ten: You counted 10 places. Ten flips have only 9 adjacent pairs.
byKey.half: You gave each place chance $\tfrac12$. Both flips must be heads: $\tfrac14$.

explain.text: Positions 1 and 2, 2 and 3, up to 9 and 10 give 9 indicators, each with chance $\tfrac14$. So $E = \tfrac94 = 2.25$, overlaps and all.

quiz.prose: Write 1 to 10 in a random order in a row. A number is a local maximum if it beats each neighbour it has.
quiz.question: What is the expected number of local maxima? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The two end places have one neighbour, the others two.

byKey.third: You gave the two ends a chance of $\tfrac13$. An end place has one neighbour, so its chance is $\tfrac12$.
byKey.half: You gave every place a chance of $\tfrac12$. An inner place must beat two neighbours.

explain.text: An inner place is the largest of three numbers with chance $\tfrac13$. An end place beats its one neighbour with chance $\tfrac12$. So $E = \tfrac83 + 1 = \tfrac{11}{3}$.

quiz.question: How many different faces do you expect to see? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One indicator per face: does it appear at least once?

byKey.three: Three dice repeat a face quite often.
byKey.one-face: That is one face's chance of appearing. Add it over all six faces.

explain.text: Face $j$ appears with chance $1 - (5/6)^3 = 91/216$. Six faces give $91/36 \approx 2.53$. It matches the smaller-of-two-dice value by coincidence.

quiz.prose: Shuffle a full deck and lay it out in a row.
quiz.question: How many adjacent pairs of cards do you expect to be both red?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. There are 51 adjacent pairs; find one pair's chance.

byKey.quarter: You used $\tfrac14$ for both red, as if with replacement. The second card is red with chance $\tfrac{25}{51}$.
byKey.half: You used one card's chance. Both cards must be red.

explain.text: Each of the 51 adjacent pairs is both red with chance $\tfrac{26}{52} \cdot \tfrac{25}{51} = \tfrac{25}{102}$. So $E = 51 \times \tfrac{25}{102} = 12.5$.
